catalog_quote: 'ਬੌਰੀਆ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ' ਵਿਚ 'ਬਲ਼' — 'ਬੌਰੀਆ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ' ਵਿਚ ਵਕਤੇ ਦੀ ਸਥਿਤੀ ਅਨੁਸਾਰ ਵਾਕ ਵਿਚ ਕਿਸੇ ਖਾਸ ਸ਼ਬਦ 'ਤੇ 'ਬਲ਼' ਦਿੱਤਾ ਜਾਂਦਾ ਹੈ। 1. ਬੌਰੀਆ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ ਵਿਚ ਸਥਿਤੀ ਅਨੁਸਾਰ 'ਬਲ਼' ਦੀ ਵਰਤੋਂ ਕੀਤੀ ਜਾਂਦੀ ਹੈ। ਜਿਸ ਸ਼ਬਦ ਉੱਪਰ 'ਬਲ਼' ਦਿੱਤਾ ਜਾਵੇ ਉਸ ਦਾ ਉਚਾਰਨ ਲੰਮਾ ਹੋ ਜਾਂਦਾ ਹੈ। ... 2. 'ਬੌਰੀਆ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ' ਵਿਚ /ਤੌ/ ਧੁਨੀ ਭਾਵ, (ਤਾਂ) ਧੁਨੀ ਦਾ ਉਚਾਰਨ ਹੁੰਦਾ ਹੈ ਤਾਂ, ਉਸ ਤੋਂ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਆਉਣ ਵਾਲੇ ਸ਼ਬਦ ਤੇ 'ਬਲ਼' ਦਿੱਤਾ ਜਾਂਦਾ ਹੈ। (i) ਹਰ੍ਹਮਨ ਤੌ ਜਾਏਗੈ। (ਹਰਮਨ ਤਾਂ ਜਾਂਦਾ ਹੈ।) ... 'ਬੌਰੀਆ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ' ਵਿਚ 'ਪੰਜਾਬੀ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ' ਵਾਂਗ 'ਬਲ਼' ਨੂੰ ਸ਼ਬਦ ਦੀ ਪੱਧਰ 'ਤੇ ਅੰਕਿਤ ਕਰਨ ਲਈ ਅੱਧਕ ( ੱ) ਲਗਾਖਰ ਦੀ ਵਰਤੋਂ ਕੀਤੀ ਜਾਂਦੀ ਹੈ। ਜਿਸ ਅੱਖਰ ਤੇ ਅੱਧਕ ਦੀ ਵਰਤੋਂ ਕੀਤੀ ਜਾਂਦੀ ਹੈ ਉਸ ਤੋਂ ਅਗਲੇ ਅੱਖਰ ਦੀ ਆਵਾਜ਼ ਦੋਹਰੀ ਹੋ ਜਾਂਦੀ ਹੈ। ਨਮੂਨਾ ਦੇਖੋ:– (i) ਪਤੋ (ਕਿਸੇ ਗੱਲ ਦਾ ਗਿਆਨ ਹੋਣਾ) ... ਪੱਤੋ (ਸਬਕ ਸਿਖਾਉਣਾ) ... (iii) ਕਦ (ਸਰੀਰ ਦੀ ਲੰਬਾਈ) ... ਕੱਦ (ਕਦੋਂ)

new_statements.translation: In the 'Bauria language', according to the speaker's situation, 'stress' is placed on some particular word in the sentence. 1. In Bauria, 'stress' is used according to the situation; the word on which 'stress' is placed is pronounced longer. [...] 2. In 'Bauria', when the sound /tau/, i.e. (taan 'indeed/then'), is pronounced, 'stress' is placed on the word that precedes it. [...] In 'Bauria', as in 'Punjabi', to mark 'stress' at the word level the addak ( ੱ ) diacritic is used; the sound of the letter following the one on which the addak is used becomes doubled.

The quoted passage is there verbatim with marked omissions, but its locator is slightly off: the heading '(ੳ) ਬਲ਼ (Stress)' and the 'ਬੌਰੀਆ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ ਵਿਚ ਬਲ਼' paragraph with rules 1 (situational emphasis, stressed word lengthened) and 2 (stress on the word before /ਤੌ/ = taan) are on printed p. 44 (pdf page 8); the addak sentence starts at the foot of p. 44 and its minimal pairs pato/patto, maghi/magghi, kad/kadd are on p. 45 (pdf page 9…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The source treats stress as sentence-level emphasis: a word is stressed (and lengthened) according to what the speaker wants to emphasise, and the word preceding the focus particle tau 'indeed' carries stress. At the word level it equates 'stress' with consonant gemination (Gurmukhi addak), illustrated by minimal pairs pato 'knowing' vs patto 'lesson', maghi vs magghi 'small pot', kad 'height' vs kadd 'when'. No rule for which syllable of a word is prominent is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only word-level remark is the gemination (addak) contrast. Separately the thesis describes a Punjabi-type three-way tone (low/mid/high, pp. 46-49) and quotes Chahal 2007 (p. 249) that tone was acquired from Punjabi.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the sentence (emphatic/focus stress) plus a word-level 'stress' that is really gemination; citation forms are not discussed. The description concerns the Bauria of Malwa Punjab (informants from Faridkot, Moga, Muktsar, Mansa, Fazilka, Bathinda, Jalandhar, Firozpur, Ludhiana, Sangrur, Patiala), heavily Punjabi-influenced. The phonological framework follows Punjabi school grammars (Cheema 2009, Harkirat Singh 1964), where 'bal' is conventionally identified with the addak; treat the reading as low-confidence.
new_statements.identity_note: Singh 2025 describes the speech of the Bauria (Baori/Bawaria) community of Punjab state, India — informants from Faridkot, Moga, Muktsar, Mansa, Fazilka, Bathinda, Jalandhar, Firozpur, Ludhiana, Sangrur and Patiala districts (Malwa Punjab). This is the same population Grierson 1907 (LSI IX.iii pp. 176-185) treated as 'Baori' of the Panjab (Lahore/Firozpur specimens) and is what Glottolog baur1251 / ISO bge covers; the Rajasthan Baori/Moghia (Kishangarh) variety is not described. The Punjab variety is heavily Punjabi-influenced and has acquired a Punjabi-type three-way tone (Singh ch. 2 pp. 46-49; Chahal 2007 p. 249 as quoted at ch. 5 p. 187).

sources.note: Ch. 2 'Bauria bhasha: dhuni-viunt', section '(u) Bal (Stress)', printed pp. 43-44: stress is placed on a particular word of the sentence according to the speaker's situation and lengthens that word; the word before the particle /tau/ (= Punjabi taan) is stressed; at word level 'stress' is what the addak (gemination) marks, with minimal pairs pato/patto 'know'/'lesson', maghi/magghi, kad/kadd. No syllable-placement rule. Repeated in ch. 4 pp. 140-141 (Bauria vs standard Punjabi; 'stress is realised on geminate consonants') and ch. 5 pp. 179-180. Tone: three tones (low/mid/high) as in Punjabi,…
